items.quote: You who are in the three companies that are going on duty on the Sabbath—a third of you guarding the royal palace, a third at the Sur Gate, and a third at the gate behind the guard, who take turns guarding the temple— and you who are in the other two companies that normally go off Sabbath duty are all to guard the temple for the king.
items.contrast: The reader must determine whether the temple-guarding command applies only to the two off-duty companies or to both the three on-duty and two off-duty companies.
items.reason: The two-company reading is plausible because that group appears immediately before the command. However, the sentence coordinates the three companies with the other two and says they are “all” to guard the temple. The key is therefore incomplete; changing it to include both groups would repair the item.

items.quote: because they had not yet come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.
items.contrast: The reader must distinguish the stated cause—the Danites lacked an inheritance—from the nearby background fact that Israel had no king.
items.reason: Israel’s lack of a king could initially seem relevant, but the explicit causal clause identifies the absence of an inheritance as the reason the Danites were seeking somewhere to settle.

items.quote: When Zebul the governor of the city heard what Gaal son of Ebed said, he was very angry. Under cover he sent messengers to Abimelek
items.contrast: The reader must resolve that “he” refers to Zebul, the angry governor, rather than to the nearby Gaal.
items.reason: Gaal is a plausible mistake because he is named immediately before the pronouns, but the sentence makes Zebul the subject who heard, became angry, and then secretly sent the messengers.

items.quote: Then he called two of his centurions and ordered them, “Get ready a detachment
items.contrast: The reader must distinguish the two centurions who receive the order from the soldiers and other personnel they are ordered to assemble.
items.reason: The two hundred soldiers are a plausible mistake because they form part of the requested detachment, but “called two of his centurions and ordered them” explicitly identifies the recipients.

items.quote: I also ordered his accusers to present to you their case against him.
items.contrast: The reader must distinguish the accusers who are ordered to present the case from the Sanhedrin, before which the man had previously appeared.
items.reason: The Sanhedrin is a plausible mistake because it is associated with the earlier accusation inquiry, but the final sentence explicitly assigns the presentation to “his accusers.” The technical stand-in “the addressee” is avoidable; “Who was ordered to present their case?” would be clearer.
